text.p: Callaway Golf Co Chief Executive and President Donald Dye said he is comfortable with Wall Street 1996 consensus estimates projecting earnings per share upwards of $1.70 and revenues of around $670 million.
Dye also said in a presentation to a Montgomery Securities investors conference here the company aims to be the number one supplier of golf putters within the next 18 months.
"We intend to be #1 in the putter market in the next 18 months," Dye told investors.

Callaway's Big Bertha metal irons, introduced in May 1994, have become the market's best-selling products and the company is seeking to extend the success with products such as its War Bird and Great Big Bertha lines of metalwoods as well as Big Bertha and S2H2 golf irons.

Dye said the company believes it can continue to develop new niche products while relying on its core product lines to drive sales as well, noting the company has produced more refined Big Bertha Gold irons and Bobby Jones putters.
After the presentation, he said the company may experiment with as many as 50 to 100 putter designs to find the feel and characteristics customers find most comfortable.
"It's like shoes...you've got to try a huge variety," he said.

Dye also said he expects a partnership with Sumimoto in Japan will help lift its sales from around $60 million to approach the $200-$400 million market opportunity which Callaway estimates it can target.
He said consensus estimates were for "EPS someplace above $1.70 for this year. We're comfortable with that." He said he was also comfortable with projected revenues of $670 million in 1996.
Callaway revenues rose 23 percent in 1995 to $553.3 million, a 10-fold increase from 1991, and the company posted earnings per share of $1.40 last year.
